title: The mind heals
hookLine: in illness, the mind can lighten the body's burden (Letters 78)
last: METRONAX — LEARN AS LONG AS I LIVE.

lines: LUCILIUS IS SICK, AND TIRED OF IT.
cards: Lucilius is sick: a lingering illness with a cough and a fever that keeps coming back, and he's tired of it. Seneca knows the feeling from the inside.
As a young man, he was ill for years with a chest complaint that wore him down to almost nothing. So the seventy-eighth letter isn't a lecture from someone who's never been in bed for a month.
It's from a fellow patient who made it through. He doesn't offer it in place of medicine. He offers what the mind can do while the body mends.

teach.b: In his long illness, Seneca says, his studies and his friends were his medicine. Friends sat with him, talked with him, cheered him. Nothing helps a sick person more, he says, than the affection of friends.
Illness brings three hard things: fear of death, bodily pain, and the loss of ordinary pleasures. The body carries the sickness. The mind can carry, or drop, much of the rest.
Then a well-known, and debatable, claim.
Very sharp pain, he says, tends not to last long; pain that lasts long tends to be milder.
The mind can withdraw some of its attention, and we make pain worse by adding complaints to it, telling ourselves how unbearable it is.
Modern doctors would add a lot to this, and chronic pain is real in ways Seneca didn't describe. The gentler point is the lasting one.
Don't add a second illness of the mind to the first of the body. Don't keep reciting your suffering to yourself. Remember brave people who bore worse.
The body heals at its own pace; the mind can keep it kind company, instead of shouting at it.

how: People who draw on Seneca in illness follow their doctors' care and also tend the mind: keeping friends close, staying interested in something, and not adding complaint to pain.

o: the soul, which leaves the body behind when you die
a Roman doctor's word for a fever that comes back
the mind, which can ease the body's load in illness

games.q: the mind in illness — tap the pairs.

s: the pain is real; his point is not to add complaint to it.
Seneca was seriously ill for years as a young man
he says studies and friends helped him through.
Seneca says we can make pain worse by adding complaint
don't add an illness of the mind to one of the body.

games.q: you've been sick for weeks and keep telling yourself how unbearable it is. what does the seventy-eighth letter suggest?
o: tell yourself more often, so you're ready.
stop adding complaint to pain, and lean on friends and interests.
games.why: Seneca says not to add a sickness of the mind to the body's, and names friends and study as his own medicine.

practice: Find one place in your body that aches or is tired today, a shoulder, your lower back, your eyes, and rest your attention there gently, the way you'd rest a hand on a friend's arm.
Notice the sensation itself, apart from the story about it, and breathe toward it. If nothing aches, simply thank a part of your body that's working well.

wordCard.voice: Animus. Seneca's word for the mind, which he says can lighten the body's burden in illness, through friends, study, and not adding complaint to pain. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the mind or spirit, which Seneca says can lighten the body's burden in illness.

carryVoice: Your line: the mind helps. Friends and study were Seneca's medicine for years. See you tomorrow.
